full_judgment:
Syed Amirul Islam, J: This Rule was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the order date 26th November, 1996 passed by the respondent No.1, Sessions Judge, Noakhaii, in Miscellaneous Case No.353 of 1996 for fresh trial of GR Case No.1 of 1983 of the Court of Magistrate, 1st Class, Noakhali should not be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and why direction should not be made for quashing proceedings against the petitioner in GR Case No.1 of 1983. 

 3. That the dead body of Ziauddin Mahmud, son of respondent No.3 was missing since 29-12-82 and the dead body was discovered on 1-1-83 whereupon CID Case No.1/83 was started with the local police. Subsequently, the SI Sagir Ahmed Suo motu lodged First Information Report on 5-1-83 and took up the investigation of the case and submitted charge sheet on 20-8-83 under sections 364/302/201 read with section 34/109 and 120B of the Penal Code and after submission of the charge-sheet the case was registered as GR Case No. 1 of 1983. When the case was pending in the Court of Sessions Judge, Noakhali for trial the case was transferred to the Special Martial Law Court No.4, Comilla by the Zonal Martial Law Administrator, Zone-D, Comilla, for trial and the said Martial Law Court on completion of trial convicted the petitioner and the other co-accused’s and sentenced them to suffer imprisonment for life by judgment dated 15-3-1994. Pursuant to that judgment the petitioner suffered RI from 15-3-1983 to 16-11-91 where after he was released from custody upon declaration of the general amnesty by the then acting President. After coming out from jail the petitioner tiled Writ Petition No.3832 of 1992 challenging the order of conviction and sentence passed by the Special Martial Law Court No. 4 in Special Martial Law Case No. 24 of 1983. The High Court Division upon hearing the parties made the Rule absolute vide Judgment dated 21-4-1994 on the ground that the trial held by the Special Martial Law Court No. 4 was malafide and coral, non judice. It appears that the petitioner also instituted Money Suit No. 3 of 1995 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Noakhali against a number of persons including respondent No. 3 claiming damages for malicious prosecution and wrongful imprisonment. It further appears that the respondent No. 3 who is defendant No. 4 in the aforesaid money suit has submitted an application before the learned Sessions Judge, Noakhali, that is respondent No. 1, praying for fresh trial of GR Case No. 1 of 1983, Noakhali, whereupon Miscellaneous Case No. 353 of 1996 was registered in the Court of the learned Sessions Judge, Noakhali and the learned Sessions Judge after hearing the learned public prosecutor passed an order on 26-11-96 for disposal of the aforesaid GR Case No. 1 of 1983 in accordance with law and sent the case record to the District Magistrate, Noakhali, with a direction to send the case record of GR Case No.1/83 to the learned Sessions Judge's Court for trial and that order is now under challenge in this petition. 

 4. Mr Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner submits that, in fact, there has been trial of the petitioner and he was convicted and sentenced to suffer rigorous imprisonment for life in GR Case No. 1 of 1983 (Special Martial Law Case No. 24 of 1985) and having suffered imprisonment for about 9 years came out of jail due to general amnesty declared by the acting President of the country and. as such, the instant case is attracted by the provisions of Article 35(2) of the Constitution and the petitioner cannot be proceeded against by way of fresh trial for the same offence of which he has already suffered rigorous imprisonment for about 9 years. Mr Ahmed alternatively argues that even if it is found that Article 35(2) of the Constitution is not attracted in the instant case then also the petitioner cannot be proceeded against by way of fresh trial in view of the fact that the petitioner was convicted by a Court and has suffered imprisonment for about 9 years for no fault of his own and in support of the contention be relies on the decision reported in 49 DLR 255 and in the course of reply Mr Khondkar Mahbubuddin Ahmed relies on the decision reported in 3 DLR (FC) 518 and submits that if the order of fresh trial is maintained that would amount to double jeopardy and his client will suffer twice for the same offence for no fault of his own. The learned Advocate also relies an the decision reported in 49 DLR (AD) 39. 

 5. Mr Muhammad Ismail, the learned Advocate appearing for the respondent No. 3, submits that in the instant case it is apparent from the judgment of the Writ Petition No. 3832 of 1992 that the trial held by the Special Martial Law Court No. 4, Zone-D, was malafide and Coram non-judice and the entire proceeding was invalid in the eye of law and the petitioner was not exonerated from the charges on merit of the case. The learned Advocate further submits that the provision as contained in Article 35(2) of the Constitution is parallel to the provisions of section 403 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and it is now. Well settled that if the case is not disposed of on merit by a competent court of law there is no bar in proceeding with the case afresh by a Competent Court. The learned Advocate further submits that the cases reported in 19 DLR 255, 3 DLR (FC) 518 and 49 DLR (AD) 32 are not applicable to the facts and circumstances of the present case. The learned Advocate further submits that in 19 DLR case the trial was held by a competent court of law but in the instant case the petitioner was tried by a court which had no jurisdiction at all to try the case. In that view of the matter the principle enunciated in 19 DLR cannot be applied in the instant case. The learned Advocate finally submits that the other two cases also have no manner of application in the facts and circumstance of the present case. 

 6. We have perused the application and the papers and documents annexed therewith. There is no dispute that the petitioner was tried by Special Martial Law Court No. 4, Zone D. Comilla and convicted and sentenced to life imprisonment. On a perusal, of the judgment passed in Writ Petition No. 3832 of 1992 it appears that the order of conviction and sentence passed by Special Martial Law Court No. 4, Comilla in Special Martial Law case No. 24 of 1983 was declared to have been passed without lawful authority and was quashed on the ground that the judgment and order of conviction and sentence was carom non judice. Since the Special Martial Law Court had no jurisdiction to try the petitioner, the judgment, conviction and sentence passed by it was a nullity and had no existence in the eye of law. 

 7. It is contended by Mr Khandaker Mahbubuddin Ahmed that even if it is found that Article 35(2) of the Constitution is not attracted because of the fact that the Special Martial Law Court had no jurisdiction to hold the trial and the conviction and sentence is a nullity, yet fact remains that there was a trial and as a result of that the petitioner has undergone imprisonment for about 9 (nine) years and, as such, in the instant case the principle laid down in 19 DLR case should be applied. This contention had been disputed by Mr Md Ismail. He, on the other hand, contended that the principle enunciated in the case Md Shafiullah vs State 19 DLR 255 cannot be applied in the present case as in that case the trial was held by a competent court but for want of sanction the prosecution was found to be incompetent and the High Court refused to pass an order of fresh trial of the accused in that Case because he suffered for no fault of his own but for the fault of the prosecution. We have considered the case of Md Shafiullah vs the State and we find that in that case the trial was held by a competent Criminal Court which found that the prosecution was void as the previous sanction of the appropriate government was not obtained and in considering the question of retrial the Court refused to pass such an order on the ground that the accused has suffered from incompetent prosecution for no fault of his own. But the facts of the present case are quite distinguishable. In the present case the GR Case No. 1 of 1983 was not transferred to the Special Martial Law Court at the instance of the prosecution rather the Zonal Martial Law Administrator Suo motu transferred the case. The said transfer of the case to the Special Martial Law Court was without jurisdiction and the Special Martial Law Court had no authority in law to try the case. Thus the entire trial was illegal and without jurisdiction and hence void. So, the trial in question was no trial in the eye of law. 

 8. Now the question that calls for determination is whether in the facts and circumstances of the case the ordinary Criminal Court has jurisdiction to proceed with the trial of GR Case No. 1 of 1983 afresh. The fundamental right which is guaranteed in Article 35(2) of the Constitution enunciates the principles of "autre fois convict" "double jeopardy". The roots of the principle are to be found in the well established rule of Common law "that where a person has been convicted of an offence by a Court of competent jurisdiction the conviction is a bar to all further criminal proceedings for the 'Same offence". (See (1890) 24 QBD 423)  To the same effect is the ancient maxim "Mime Bis Debet Puniri Pro Uno Delecto"; that is to say, that no one ought to be twice punished for one offence or as it is sometimes written "Pro Eadem causa" that is, for the same Cause. 

 “………….nor shall any person be subject for the same offence to be twice put in jeopardy of life or limb; nor shall be compelled, in any Criminal Case, to be witness against himself……………” 

 14. The word "prosecuted" is introduced in the present case in order to make it clear that the power relates to punishment by a Court of law and not to other kinds of punishment besides a judicial penalty. The word "and" has been used in conjunctive and not a disjunctive sense. The principle that no citizen should he put in jeopardy of his life or liberty more than once is so well known that in almost every constitution one finds a provision against a person being put to trial in respect of the same offence more than once. Section 403, Criminal Procedure Code is nothing more than an elaboration of this principle in all its notices and distinctions. What the framers of the Constitution wanted to provide for was specific thing, namely, the non-prosecution of a person who had already been prosecuted and convicted. 

 15. We have already noted that Article 35(2) uses the conjunction "and" and not the disjunction "or" between the words "prosecuted" and "punished" and this makes it clear that to bar a fresh prosecution for the same offence, the accused should have been both prosecuted and punished. So, when as accused is discharged for want of sanction there is no punishment and when a man is punished departmentally there is no prosecution. So also is the case where the prosecution is void for want of jurisdiction; there is no prosecution nor there is any punishment. Thus Article 35(2) of the Constitution does not take away the right to institute a second prosecution when the first is found to be a nullity by reason of want of jurisdiction. 

 16. In the case of Yusuf Ali Mulla vs King (AIR 1949 PC 264) the Privy Council held that where there was no valid sanction for the prosecution of the accused the prosecution was a nullity and the order of the Magistrate acquitting the accused (or convicting as the case may be) was without jurisdiction and could only operate as an order of discharge; the accused had not been tried by a court of competent jurisdiction and accordingly section 403(1) of the Criminal Procedure Code was no bar to the institution of a fresh prosecution against the accused for the same offence on the same facts as in the former prosecution. We may also note the fact that even under the Common law, a plea of autre foil acquit or autre fois convict can only be raised where the first trial was before a Court competent to pass a valid order of acquittal or conviction and that unless the earlier trial was a lawful one which might have resulted in a conviction the accused was never in jeopardy (RV Bates, (1911)1K B 964). 

 17. Thus the whole basis of section 403(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure as well as Article 35(2) is that the first trial should have been before a Court competent to hear and determine the case and to record a verdict of conviction or acquittal; if the court is not so competent, the whole trial is null and void and it cannot be said that there was any conviction or acquittal in force within the meaning of section 403(1) Criminal Procedure Code or Article 35(2) of the Constitution. Such a trial does not bar a subsequent trial of the accused. 

 19. Mr Khondkar Mahbubuddin Ahmed submitted that even if the case does not come within the scope of Article 35(2) of the Constitution, the principle enunciated in the 19 DLR case should be applied because the petitioner has already suffered imprisonment for about nine years due to the verdict of the Special Martial Law Court No.4 though the prosecution is a nullity in the eye of law. But we find it difficult to accept the submission because it is now well settled that either to attract Article 35(2) of the Constitution or the provisions of section 403(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure the first trial must have been before a Court competent to hear and determine the case and to record a verdict of conviction or acquittal. In the instant case the prosecution was incompetent and void for want of jurisdiction. So was in the 19 DLR case. In the 19 DLR case the High Court did not pass an order of retrial on the ground that the accused suffered from incompetent prosecution for no fault of his own but for the fault of the prosecution but in the present case the prosecution was not at fault. The case was not transferred to the Special Martial Law Court at the instance of the prosecution rather the Zonal Martial Law Administrator suo motu transferred the case to that Court. The prosecution had no role to play in the matter of transfer of the case. 

 20. Mr Khondaker Mahbubuddin Ahmed also submitted that rightly or wrongly the petitioner was convicted by the Special Martial Law Court and he had suffered imprisonment of long nine years and, as such, it will not be expedient that the case should now be prosecuted afresh. This argument drawn from misery is a good argument for being considered at the end of the case and in the event of this petitioner being convicted it will he open to the trial Court to take a lenient view at the time of passing the sentence. This is certainly no ground for not getting along with the trial. The cases relied on by Mr Ahmed have no manner of application to the facts and circumstances of the present one. In the premises we do not find any illegality in the impugned order.
